problems.title: Calculate in the correct order
problems.question: Evaluate $\dfrac{(-1\frac{2}{15}+6\frac{1}{12})\div0.5+2.5}{2.4\cdot1.3-1.88}$.
problems.idea: Work out the brackets first, then the numerator and denominator separately.
formulas: $m\frac{p}{q}=\frac{mq+p}{q}$; a minus sign in front of a mixed number applies to the whole number.
$\frac{a}{b}+\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ad+bc}{bd}$; dividing by $0.5$ is multiplying by $2$.
steps: Convert the mixed numbers: $-1\frac{2}{15}=-\frac{17}{15}$ and $6\frac{1}{12}=\frac{73}{12}$.
The denominator is $2.4\cdot1.3-1.88=3.12-1.88=1.24$.

problems.title: Find the whole route from the last part
problems.question: Tourists travel 7/22 of their route on day 1, one third of what remains on day 2, and the final 25 km on day 3. Find the route length.
problems.idea: Keep track of fractions of the whole route, not just fractions of the remainder.
formulas: Remaining fraction $=1-\text{fraction already travelled}$.
Part $=\text{fraction}\times\text{whole}$, so whole $=\text{part}\div\text{fraction}$.
steps: After day 1, $1-\frac{7}{22}=\frac{15}{22}$ of the route remains.
Day 2 leaves $\frac{2}{3}$ of that remainder. Thus day 3 covers $\frac23\cdot\frac{15}{22}=\frac5{11}$ of the whole route.
If the route is $L$ km, then $\frac5{11}L=25$. Therefore $L=25\cdot\frac{11}{5}=55$.
Check: day 1 is $17.5$ km, day 2 is $12.5$ km, and day 3 is $25$ km; these add to $55$ km.

problems.title: When exactly two buses return
problems.question: Three buses return to their station every 3, 4, and 8 hours. They leave together. When are exactly two back at the station for the first time?
problems.idea: Compare the earliest common return time for each pair, and check that the third bus is absent.
formulas: Two repeating schedules with periods $a,b$ coincide after $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$ hours.
steps: The 3-hour and 4-hour buses first meet after $\operatorname{lcm}(3,4)=12$ hours.
The 3-hour and 8-hour buses first meet after $\operatorname{lcm}(3,8)=24$ hours.
The 4-hour and 8-hour buses first meet after $\operatorname{lcm}(4,8)=8$ hours, the earliest of these.
At 8 hours, the 3-hour bus has not returned: its return times are $3,6,9,\ldots$. Exactly two buses are present.

problems.title: Find the last digit of a large power
problems.question: What is the last digit of $777^{222}$?
problems.idea: Only the last digit of the base affects the last digit of its powers.
formulas: The last digits of $7^n$ repeat with period $4$: $7,9,3,1$.
$n=4q+r$ determines the position in the repeating cycle.
steps: Since 777 ends in 7, use the cycle for powers of 7.
$222=4\cdot55+2$. The exponent has remainder 2, so use the second entry of the cycle.

problems.title: What a digit sum of 12 tells us
problems.question: A natural number has digit sum 12. Decide which statements in the test must be true.
problems.idea: Use divisibility by 3 and 9, and check every option rather than assuming there is only one correct statement.
formulas: A natural number is divisible by $3$ or $9$ exactly when its digit sum is divisible by that number.
If $N=m^2$ and $3\mid N$, then $3\mid m$, hence $9\mid N$.
steps: The digit sum 12 is divisible by 3, but not by 9. Therefore $3\mid N$ and $9\nmid N$.
Suppose $N$ were a square. A square divisible by 3 must be divisible by 9, contradicting the previous step. Thus $N$ is not a perfect square.
Also, $N>3$ and is divisible by 3, so it has a divisor other than 1 and itself: it is composite.
The number need not be even or divisible by 4: $39$ has digit sum 12 and is neither.
problems.answer: Both “not a natural-number square” (დ) and “composite” (ვ) are true.
problems.note: The printed question has two true options. A single-answer key cannot make one of these mathematical statements false.

problems.title: Reduce a remainder to a smaller divisor
problems.question: A has remainder 15 when divided by 18. Find its remainder when divided by 9.
problems.idea: Write A as a multiple of 18 plus its remainder.
formulas: Division with remainder: $A=dq+r$, with $0\le r<d$.
steps: The condition means $A=18q+15$ for some integer $q$.
The remainder is 6 because $0\le6<9$.

problems.title: Use the divisibility tests for 45
problems.question: How many five-digit numbers $24A4B$ are divisible by 45?
problems.idea: A multiple of 45 must be divisible by both 5 and 9.
formulas: $45=5\cdot9$, with 5 and 9 having no common factor.
Divisibility by 5 requires last digit 0 or 5; divisibility by 9 requires digit sum a multiple of 9.
steps: The digit sum is $2+4+A+4+B=10+A+B$.
If $B=0$, then $10+A$ must be a multiple of 9. Since $A$ is a digit, the only possibility is $10+A=18$, giving $A=8$.
If $B=5$, then $15+A=18$, giving $A=3$.
The two numbers are $24840$ and $24345$. Check: $24840=45\cdot552$ and $24345=45\cdot541$.

problems.title: Count the positive divisors
problems.question: How many positive divisors does $2^5\cdot3^4\cdot7^{14}$ have?
problems.idea: A divisor is determined by choosing an exponent for each prime factor.
formulas: For $N=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}$, the divisor count is $d(N)=(a_1+1)\cdots(a_k+1)$.
steps: The exponent of 2 in a divisor may be any of $0,1,\ldots,5$: 6 choices.
The exponent of 3 has 5 choices, from 0 through 4.
The exponent of 7 has 15 choices, from 0 through 14.
These choices are independent, so the count is $6\cdot5\cdot15=450$. The divisor 1 is included by choosing all three exponents zero.

problems.title: Count the trailing zeroes of a factorial
problems.question: How many zeroes end the product $1\cdot2\cdots125=125!$?
problems.idea: Every trailing zero needs a factor 10, made from one factor 2 and one factor 5. Factors of 5 are the limiting supply.
formulas: The number of factors of 5 in $n!$ is $\left\lfloor\frac n5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n{25}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n{125}\right\rfloor+\cdots$.
steps: There are $\lfloor125/5\rfloor=25$ multiples of 5, each providing at least one factor 5.
The 5 multiples of 25 provide an additional factor 5 each.
The number 125 provides one more factor 5, because $125=5^3$.
Total: $25+5+1=31$. There are more than enough factors of 2 to pair with them.

problems.title: Advance a weekday using remainders
problems.question: August 1 is Sunday. What weekday is December 27 in the same year?
problems.idea: Only the number of extra days after whole weeks changes the weekday.
formulas: $D=7q+r$ means advancing $D$ days advances the weekday by $r$ places.
steps: From August 1 to August 31 is 30 days. Then count 30 days in September, 31 in October, 30 in November, and 27 in December.
$148=7\cdot21+1$, so the weekday advances by one day.
One day after Sunday is Monday.

problems.title: Remainders of a linear expression
problems.question: When divided by 7, $a$ has remainder 6 and $b$ has remainder 4. Find the remainder of $2a+5b$.
problems.idea: Separate the multiples of 7 from the small leftover part.
formulas: A multiple of 7 contributes remainder 0.
steps: Substitute: $2a+5b=2(7m+6)+5(7n+4)$.
Collect terms: $2a+5b=7(2m+5n)+32$.
Since $32=7\cdot4+4$, this becomes $7(2m+5n+4)+4$.

problems.title: A proposed inequality must work for every allowed value
problems.question: Without any extra condition on $a$, which strict ordering of $a,a^2,a^3$ must hold?
problems.idea: One counterexample is enough to disprove a statement claimed to hold always.
steps: Every proposed ordering in options ა–ე uses strict inequalities.
Choose the allowed value $a=1$. All three quantities equal 1, so every strict ordering is false.
The order also changes with the value of $a$: for $a=2$, $a<a^2<a^3$, while for $a=\frac12$, $a^3<a^2<a$.
problems.answer: No listed strict ordering is always true (option ვ).

problems.title: Count two overlapping groups once
problems.question: Among 100 students, 80 like mathematics, 35 like biology, and 23 like both. How many like neither?
problems.idea: Adding the two group sizes counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.
formulas: $|M\cup B|=|M|+|B|-|M\cap B|$.
$\text{Neither}=\text{Total}-|M\cup B|$.
steps: The number liking at least one subject is $80+35-23=92$.
Subtract from the group total: $100-92=8$.
Check the four disjoint groups: mathematics only $80-23=57$; biology only $35-23=12$; both 23; neither 8. Their sum is 100.

problems.title: Count fractions between two endpoints
problems.question: How many fractions with denominator 120 lie strictly between $\frac38$ and $\frac25$?
problems.idea: Put both endpoints over the required denominator, then count the integer numerators between them.
formulas: $\frac ab=\frac{ak}{bk}$ for nonzero $k$.
With the same positive denominator, fractions are ordered by their numerators.
steps: A fraction $n/120$ lies strictly between them exactly when $45<n<48$.
The integer choices are 46 and 47. The fractions are $46/120$ and $47/120$; they need not be written in lowest terms.

problems.title: Remove the overlap from a set
problems.question: Which shaded region represents $A\setminus(A\cap B)$?
problems.idea: Start with all of A and remove the elements also in B.
formulas: $A\setminus C=\{x:x\in A\text{ and }x\notin C\}$.
$A\setminus(A\cap B)=A\setminus B$.
steps: The intersection $A\cap B$ is the lens-shaped overlap of the two circles.
Removing that overlap from A leaves only the part of A outside B.
An element already in A is outside $A\cap B$ exactly when it is outside B. This explains the identity in the formulas.
Choose the diagram shading the left circle except for the shared lens: the top-right diagram among the choices.

problems.title: Consider both possible point orders
problems.question: A, B, and C lie on a line, with AB = 7 cm and BC = 9 cm. Find all possible values of AC.
problems.idea: The answer depends on whether A and C lie on opposite sides of B or on the same side.
formulas: For consecutive collinear segments, the total length is the sum.
For segments from the same starting point in the same direction, the distance between endpoints is the absolute difference.
steps: If B lies between A and C, $AC=AB+BC=7+9=16$ cm.
If A and C are on the same side of B, $AC=|BC-AB|=|9-7|=2$ cm.
The stated lengths allow both arrangements, so neither value can be discarded.

problems.title: Use the sum and difference of distances
problems.question: M, N, and K lie on a line. NK = 6 cm and MN + MK = 9 cm. Find the shorter of MN and MK.
problems.idea: First decide whether M lies inside or outside segment NK.
formulas: If M is between N and K, $MN+MK=NK$.
If M is outside NK, $\text{longer distance}-\text{shorter distance}=NK$.
steps: M cannot lie between N and K, because that would give $MN+MK=6$, not 9.
Let the shorter distance be $x$. The longer distance is $x+6$.
The sum condition gives $x+(x+6)=9$, so $2x=3$ and $x=1.5$.

problems.title: Count sectors made by concurrent lines
problems.question: Ten distinct straight lines pass through one point. Into how many regions do they divide the plane?
problems.idea: Each line contributes two rays from the common point.
formulas: $n$ distinct lines through one point make $2n$ sectors.
steps: Each of the 10 lines has two opposite rays, giving $2\cdot10=20$ rays.
In circular order around the common point, every pair of consecutive rays bounds one sector. The final ray and the first ray also bound a sector.
Therefore there are as many sectors as rays: 20.

problems.title: Turn a segment ratio into lengths
problems.question: On segment AB, AC : CD : DB = 2 : 6 : 3. The midpoints of AC and CD are 12 cm apart. Find AB.
problems.idea: Use one common scale factor for all three parts.
formulas: Write $AC=2t$, $CD=6t$, $DB=3t$, where $t>0$.
A midpoint divides a segment into two equal parts.
steps: Let P be the midpoint of AC and Q the midpoint of CD. Along the line the order is A, P, C, Q, D, B.
Then $PC=AC/2=t$ and $CQ=CD/2=3t$.
Thus $PQ=PC+CQ=4t=12$, giving $t=3$ cm.
Finally, $AB=AC+CD+DB=(2+6+3)t=11\cdot3=33$ cm.

problems.title: Add angles carefully and check the ray arrangement
problems.question: $\angle AOB=88^\circ52\prime$ and $\angle BOC=91^\circ15\prime$. Find $\angle AOC$.
problems.idea: Angle arithmetic uses 60 minutes per degree. The location of the rays also matters.
formulas: $1^\circ=60\prime$ and a full turn is $360^\circ$.
For opposite-side rays, the two sectors between OA and OC sum to $360^\circ$.
steps: For A and C on opposite sides of OB, adding the given sectors gives $88^\circ52\prime+91^\circ15\prime=179^\circ67\prime=180^\circ07\prime$.
This is the larger, reflex sector. The smaller angle is $360^\circ-180^\circ07\prime=359^\circ60\prime-180^\circ07\prime=179^\circ53\prime$.
If A and C instead lie on the same side of OB, the smaller angle is the difference: $91^\circ15\prime-88^\circ52\prime=2^\circ23\prime$.
problems.answer: The listed answer is $179^\circ53\prime$ (option ა), for the opposite-side arrangement.
problems.note: The wording supplies no diagram or explicit ray arrangement. Without that assumption, the angle is not uniquely determined; the same-side arrangement gives 2°23′.

problems.title: Distances between two midpoints
problems.question: From A in the same direction, AB = 40 cm and AC = 60 cm. Find the distance between the midpoints of AB and AC.
problems.idea: Measure both midpoints from the same origin A.
formulas: For a segment of length $L$, its midpoint is $L/2$ from either endpoint.
Distance on a line $=|x_2-x_1|$.
steps: Let P and Q be the midpoints of AB and AC. Then $AP=40/2=20$ cm and $AQ=60/2=30$ cm.
Both midpoints lie on the same ray from A. Hence $PQ=|30-20|=10$ cm.

problems.title: Count the lines determined by points on a circle
problems.question: Seven distinct points lie on a circle. How many lines are determined by pairs of these points?
problems.idea: Choose a pair of points, and correct for counting the two orders of that pair.
formulas: $\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2$.
A straight line meets a circle in at most two points.
steps: There are 7 choices for a first point and 6 choices for a different second point: $7\cdot6=42$ ordered pairs.
The pair A, B and the pair B, A determine the same line, so divide by 2: $42/2=21$.
No three of these circle points are collinear, so different unordered pairs do not create duplicate lines.

problems.title: Split an angle in a ratio
problems.question: A ray divides a $120^\circ$ angle into two parts. One is $3/5$ of the other. Find the larger angle.
problems.idea: Represent the two parts as 3 equal units and 5 equal units.
formulas: For adjacent parts, $\text{whole angle}=\text{first part}+\text{second part}$.
If small $=\frac35$ large, write small $=3t$ and large $=5t$.
steps: The angle sum gives $3t+5t=120^\circ$.
Thus $8t=120^\circ$ and $t=15^\circ$.
The larger part is $5t=75^\circ$. Check: the smaller is $45^\circ$, and $45/75=3/5$.

problems.title: Intersect two rays on a line
problems.question: Two rays lie on one straight line. Which listed type of set cannot be their intersection?
problems.idea: A ray continues forever in one direction but has an endpoint in the other direction.
formulas: A ray on a number line has the form $[a,\infty)$ or $(-\infty,a]$.
The intersection must be a subset of each original ray.
steps: The intersection cannot be the entire straight line: neither ray itself contains the entire line.
Other possibilities do occur. $[0,\infty)\cap[1,\infty)=[1,\infty)$ is a ray.
$[0,\infty)\cap(-\infty,2]=[0,2]$ is a segment, and using endpoint 0 instead of 2 gives the single point $\{0\}$. Disjoint rays can also give the empty set.
problems.answer: A complete straight line is impossible (option ა).
problems.note: The option “a union of two rays” is imprecise as a set category: such a union may itself be one ray when one ray contains the other. The clearly impossible listed set is the entire line.

problems.title: Count intersections of four nonparallel lines
problems.question: Four distinct lines lie in a plane, with no two parallel. How many distinct intersection points can they have?
problems.idea: Start with the six pairs of lines, then consider whether three or four lines meet at one point.
formulas: The number of pairs is $\binom42=\frac{4\cdot3}{2}=6$.
Three concurrent lines have three pairwise intersections but only one distinct intersection point.
steps: If no three lines meet at one point, all six pairs give different intersections: 6 points.
If exactly three lines meet at P, the fourth line meets those three at three other distinct points. Total: $1+3=4$.
If all four meet at P, there is just 1 point.
Two different triple-concurrency points are impossible with only four lines: the two triples would share two lines, forcing those two distinct lines to meet twice.
